title: Northbridge AI Platform - procurement/security review: incident comms + status page expectations

Redwood to share a preview of the proposed public status page component taxonomy (product area x region) and definitions

transcript:
Meeting header
Date: 2025-11-06
Time: 9:00 AM - 9:43 AM PT
Duration: 43 minutes
Organizer: Rachel Kim (Redwood Inference)
Attendees (Redwood): Rachel Kim, Dev Patel, Wei Chen, Kira Thompson, Michael Grant
Attendees (Northbridge AI Platform): Lena Ortiz, Samir Shah, Emily Brooks, Tom Wallace

Auto Summary (Fireflies)
- Northbridge requested more precise availability reporting than a single “API” component, specifically per-capability (streaming vs embeddings) and per-region.
- Northbridge asked for faster first public updates during incidents and consistent post-incident summaries suitable for audits.
- Redwood described an in-flight initiative to standardize status page components, add templates for each incident phase, and improve publishable post-incident summaries, without over-promising fixed SLAs.
- Next steps: Redwood to share draft templates and example summary format; Northbridge to share their required notification fields and timeline expectations; follow-up with SRE for signal mapping details.

Topics
1) What Northbridge needs from public status and incident communications
2) Component-level granularity (product surface + region + failure mode) and edge cases
3) Time-to-first-update expectations and approval/consistency constraints
4) Post-incident summaries: what gets published, timing, and confidentiality

Questions captured
- Can you separate “Streaming degraded” from “Chat completions OK” publicly?
- How do you avoid the status page flapping during transient spikes?
- For Dedicated / private VPC, do incidents appear on the public page or only in direct comms?
- What minimum fields will your post-incident summaries contain?

Transcript
[00:00] Rachel Kim: Okay, cool. I think we’re good to start. Thanks everyone for making time. This is basically the procurement and security review, but focused on incident communications and the status page. I’m Rachel, I run enterprise customer success at Redwood.

[00:14] Lena Ortiz: Thanks Rachel. I’m Lena, procurement. We’re at the stage where our risk team is like, “we need to see how you communicate outages.”

[00:22] Samir Shah: Samir, security. And Tom is IT risk.

[00:25] Tom Wallace: Hey.

[00:26] Emily Brooks: Emily, platform engineering. I’m the one who gets paged when our app errors, so I’m probably going to be annoying.

[00:33] Rachel Kim: Please be annoying. That’s the point.

[00:36] Dev Patel: Hey all, Dev here. I run support ops at Redwood.

[00:39] Wei Chen: Wei, I help with customer-facing incident language and docs.

[00:42] Kira Thompson: Kira, I’m on the enterprise side for Dedicated and Private deployments and what we can and can’t show publicly.

[00:48] Michael Grant: Michael, legal review for public summaries.

[00:53] Rachel Kim: Great. Lena, do you want to kick with what you need to sign off?

[00:58] Lena Ortiz: Sure. Two main things. One: your current status page is pretty high level. It’s like “API” and “Console” and that’s it. That doesn’t help our incident response because embeddings can be down while chat is okay, and we don’t know. Two: speed. We’ve been burned by vendors who don’t post anything for like 45 minutes and then it’s already all over Twitter. We need faster, consistent updates.

[01:23] Emily Brooks: Yeah, and not just “we are investigating.” Like, what’s impacted: region, endpoints, percentage errors, or at least, is it streaming only. We use streaming heavily.

[01:34] Rachel Kim: That’s fair. To level set: our public status page today is too coarse. We agree. Internally we have the signal breakdown by region/capability, but the public components don’t reflect it.

[01:46] Samir Shah: When you say “signal,” do you mean you actually have per-region SLOs?

[01:50] Rachel Kim: Internally we do, yes. But what we expose publicly is what we’re tightening up right now.

[01:55] Emily Brooks: Right, and we don’t want you to expose anything sensitive, but “US-East streaming degraded” is not sensitive.

[02:02] Kira Thompson: Mostly agree. The tricky bit is when it’s Dedicated or Private, and the blast radius is basically one customer, then public posting gets weird.

[02:11] Emily Brooks: Sure, if it’s only us, that’s not a public incident. But if it’s your hosted platform, we need granularity.

[02:18] Dev Patel: Also from support’s perspective, we get tickets like “status says all green but embeddings are failing.” That’s one of the top escalations we’re trying to reduce.

[02:27] Lena Ortiz: Exactly.

[02:29] Rachel Kim: Okay, so let’s talk about how we’re approaching it. We’re rolling out a component taxonomy. Think: Hosted API separated into Chat/Completions, Streaming, Embeddings, Reranking. Then segmented by region where it matters, like US-East, US-West, EU, etc.

[02:49] Emily Brooks: Are you planning like per model too? Or just capability.

[02:53] Rachel Kim: Not per model publicly, at least not initially. Capability + region is the main axis.

[02:59] Samir Shah: How do you handle partial degradation? Like p95 latency high but errors okay.

[03:05] Wei Chen: That’s where language and thresholds matter. “Degraded performance” is a separate state from “partial outage.” And we’re standardizing when we use each so it’s not arbitrary.

[03:16] Emily Brooks: I hate “degraded performance” because it can mean anything.

[03:20] Wei Chen: Totally. In the template we include something measurable when we can: “elevated error rates” vs “elevated latency.” But we also try not to spam numbers that might change minute to minute.

[03:35] Tom Wallace: For risk, we just need consistency and evidence you have a process.

[03:40] Rachel Kim: Process-wise, we are formalizing roles during incidents: incident commander, comms lead, and a scribe. The comms lead is accountable for status updates.

[03:52] Lena Ortiz: How fast do they update?

[03:54] Rachel Kim: We don’t want to commit to a hard SLA in a procurement doc right now, but we do have an internal target for time-to-first-update. Practically, we aim to post an initial “Investigating” update quickly once we confirm customer impact.

[04:10] Emily Brooks: “Quickly” is like, ten minutes, not an hour.

[04:13] Dev Patel: Yeah, the goal is to be in the “minutes, not hours” category. Also we’re automating a lot of the drafting so the comms lead isn’t writing from scratch.

[04:23] Samir Shah: Automation as in a bot?

[04:25] Dev Patel: Yes, an incident bot that prompts for the affected component and region, then pre-fills a draft update using a template, and nudges if an update hasn’t been posted.

[04:37] Emily Brooks: That sounds good. But the key is accuracy. If your status page says embeddings are down and actually it’s streaming, we’re still in trouble.

[04:45] Rachel Kim: Totally. Part of this effort is mapping internal services and metrics to public components in a deterministic way and validating it. Also anti-flap behavior so it doesn’t switch green/red every two minutes.

[04:58] Samir Shah: Anti-flap meaning hysteresis? Like you need sustained breach.

[05:01] Rachel Kim: Exactly. Sustained breach windows, plus different thresholds for “degraded” vs “outage.”

[05:08] Emily Brooks: Okay. Can I ask a concrete example? Say US-East streaming starts disconnecting, but non-streaming calls are okay. Today you’d probably mark “API degraded” and that creates panic. I want just “Streaming US-East degraded.”

[05:24] Wei Chen: That is literally one of the examples we used when drafting the templates. The update would say: “We’re investigating elevated disconnects affecting streaming responses in US-East. Non-streaming requests are not impacted at this time.”

[05:37] Emily Brooks: Perfect. That’s what I need.

[05:40] Lena Ortiz: And would that be on your public status page or would we get an email?

[05:45] Rachel Kim: For hosted, public status page. For Dedicated and Private, it depends on the scope. Kira can explain.

[05:52] Kira Thompson: Yeah, so: if it’s a generally available hosted component, that’s public. If it’s a Dedicated cluster issue that impacts multiple customers or a shared control plane function, we may post a broader component, like “Dedicated control plane degraded” but we’re careful not to expose customer-specific capacity or topology. If it’s a single-tenant private deployment, we generally do direct customer comms rather than a public page.

[06:15] Tom Wallace: That’s acceptable. We just need to see that you have documented criteria for when it’s public vs private.

[06:22] Michael Grant: From legal side, we want to avoid any disclosure that could be interpreted as “we guarantee X availability” or details that reveal a specific customer’s configuration.

[06:33] Emily Brooks: Fine, but don’t hide behind legal for basic transparency.

[06:37] Michael Grant: Agree. The goal is clarity without over-disclosure.

[06:41] Rachel Kim: Maybe it’s helpful if we describe the structure of an incident update. Wei, do you want to walk through the phases?

[06:48] Wei Chen: Sure. We use five primary states: Investigating, Identified, Mitigating, Monitoring, Resolved. Each has a template with “what we know” and “what we’re doing,” and a section for “customer impact” that forces region + component selection.

[07:07] Wei Chen: Investigating is intentionally cautious: acknowledge, describe symptoms, list affected components/regions, and set expectation for next update.

[07:16] Lena Ortiz: Do you put “next update in 30 minutes” type language?

[07:19] Wei Chen: We say something like “we’ll provide another update within X minutes” when we can. We try not to promise if we’re in a really fluid situation, but the template encourages a cadence.

[07:31] Dev Patel: And from support: we mirror that language in support macros so tickets don’t drift from the status page.

[07:38] Emily Brooks: That’s actually huge. Vendors often have support saying one thing and status page saying another.

[07:44] Rachel Kim: Exactly what we’re trying to fix.

[07:47] Samir Shah: For audits, we also need post-incident summaries. What do you publish and how fast.

[07:54] Rachel Kim: We’re standardizing that too. The summary format includes: impact, timeline, root cause class (not necessarily the full gory details), mitigation, and preventative actions. We aim to publish promptly once we’ve confirmed accuracy.

[08:10] Tom Wallace: Root cause class meaning like “dependency failure” vs “configuration change” vs “capacity.”

[08:15] Rachel Kim: Exactly. Enough to be useful without exposing sensitive internals.

[08:20] Emily Brooks: I’d also want “workarounds.” Like, did you enable fallback models, did you throttle, did you disable streaming.

[08:26] Wei Chen: We include “customer actions / workarounds” when applicable. Sometimes there isn’t a customer action other than retry, but we’ll say that.

[08:35] Samir Shah: Do you include data exposure analysis in the summary?

[08:38] Michael Grant: If there’s a security implication, we handle it via our security incident process and customer notifications. For typical availability incidents, we usually state “no evidence of data exposure” only if it’s been confirmed, otherwise we avoid speculative statements.

[08:56] Samir Shah: That’s reasonable.

[08:58] Emily Brooks: Can you share examples? Like a good one.

[09:00] Rachel Kim: Yes. We can share the format and redacted examples.

[09:05] Lena Ortiz: Okay, but back to the status page. Component-level: do you plan to add regions immediately? Because our requirement is at least US-East and EU.

[09:15] Rachel Kim: The plan is phased. First, break out capability components; second, add region splits for high-traffic regions. I don’t want to set dates on this call, but it’s actively in flight.

[09:27] Emily Brooks: What’s “in flight” mean? Like this quarter.

[09:31] Rachel Kim: Yes, we’re working on it now.

[09:34] Dev Patel: Also, a lot of the work is to ensure the mapping is correct. It’s not just rearranging UI. It’s also making sure internal tagging supports “this request is embeddings” vs “this request is streaming.”

[09:48] Emily Brooks: That’s the other thing. Some vendors can’t tell which endpoint is failing.

[09:52] Rachel Kim: We can, but we need to make it consistent across services so the public components match reality.

[10:00] Samir Shah: How do you prevent flapping? If it’s tied to an error rate, sometimes it spikes for two minutes.

[10:07] Rachel Kim: We use sustained windows plus “clear” thresholds that are lower than “trigger” thresholds. So it’s harder to flip back to green instantly. And we keep manual override as an option.

[10:20] Emily Brooks: Manual override being someone can mark it degraded even if the signal hasn’t tripped.

[10:24] Rachel Kim: Yes, for example if we have strong evidence from internal debugging or customer reports.

[10:30] Dev Patel: But we want to avoid making on-call do a ton of clicking. So the bot helps, and we have a runbook.

[10:37] Lena Ortiz: On approval: do updates need legal review?

[10:40] Michael Grant: Not for every update. Templates are pre-approved. For high-severity or anything that might implicate security or contractual language, there’s an approval step, usually incident commander + support lead, and legal if needed. But the intent is not to slow down initial comms.

[10:58] Tom Wallace: Good.

[11:01] Emily Brooks: Another thing: titles. I’ve seen “API issues” and it’s meaningless. We want titles like “Elevated errors for Embeddings in US-East.”

[11:10] Wei Chen: Yep, template includes a title pattern: [Component] [Region] [Symptom]. Not always perfect, but that’s the goal.

[11:20] Rachel Kim: Can you share your minimum requirements? Like what your internal incident comms expects.

[11:26] Emily Brooks: Minimum: start time, detection time, impacted regions, impacted endpoints/capabilities, severity (even if it’s your own label), mitigations, customer-facing workaround. And updates every, say, 30 minutes until resolved.

[11:45] Lena Ortiz: And for procurement: we need an expectation for first notification. Our internal policy is 15 minutes for Sev1-type events, but I understand you may not commit.

[11:56] Rachel Kim: We hear you. We can provide our internal targets and process, but we’ll avoid putting a hard SLA in the MSA unless there’s a negotiated SLA addendum.

[12:08] Lena Ortiz: That’s fine. Just don’t be vague.

[12:10] Rachel Kim: Understood.

[12:12] Samir Shah: Also: how do you handle third-party dependencies, like cloud region issues.

[12:18] Wei Chen: We call out dependency impact when it’s confirmed. In early phases we avoid blaming a cloud provider unless we have strong evidence. But we can say “We’re investigating an upstream networking issue impacting US-East” if that’s the situation.

[12:34] Emily Brooks: Good. Don’t do the “it’s AWS” thing with no proof.

[12:38] Dev Patel: (laughs) Yeah, agreed.

[12:40] Rachel Kim: A quick check: you mentioned status page granularity and speed. Anything else blocking?

[12:46] Tom Wallace: We want to know where post-incident summaries live. Public page? Portal?

[12:51] Rachel Kim: Plan is: the incident page includes the timeline and then links to a post-incident summary once it’s available. For some enterprise customers, we can also provide a direct PDF-like summary on request, but generally it’s on the status site.

[13:09] Samir Shah: If it’s on public site, does it contain any customer-identifying info.

[13:13] Michael Grant: No. It’s written to be publishable, no customer names, no tenant identifiers, no precise capacity numbers.

[13:22] Emily Brooks: Okay.

[13:24] Rachel Kim: I’m going to jump us to next steps since we’re at time. Wei can share templates. Dev can share the escalation view. Kira can share Dedicated vs Private guidance. And then we’ll schedule a technical follow-up with SRE to go deeper on mapping and signals.

[13:41] Lena Ortiz: Can you include something we can attach to our internal vendor risk file? Like a one-pager.

[13:46] Rachel Kim: Yes, we can provide a short overview: roles, update phases, what gets posted publicly, and where summaries live.

[13:54] Emily Brooks: And can you include a sample incident timeline? Like the types of updates.

[13:58] Wei Chen: Yep. I’ll send a redacted example and the template blocks.

[14:03] Samir Shah: And include anything on how you decide “partial outage” vs “degraded.”

[14:07] Rachel Kim: We can include the definitions, yes.

[14:10] Tom Wallace: Great.

[14:12] Rachel Kim: Anything else before we close?

[14:15] Emily Brooks: Just one. When will the component-level status page be live? Like, I need to tell my leadership whether this is real.

[14:23] Rachel Kim: It’s real and it’s underway. I don’t want to give you a date on this call and then miss it. What I can do is: in the follow-up with SRE we can show you the proposed component list and how it maps, and give a rollout view.

[14:38] Emily Brooks: Okay, that works.

[14:40] Lena Ortiz: Thanks everyone.

[14:42] Rachel Kim: Thanks all. We’ll follow up by email with the templates and schedule.

(Transcript continues - audio ended early due to recording stop)

[15:05] Rachel Kim: Sorry, Fireflies is saying it’s stopping. We’re still here though. Quick recap: Wei sends templates tomorrow, Dev sends escalation approach, Kira sends visibility guidance, and I’ll coordinate SRE follow-up.

[15:20] Emily Brooks: Sounds good.

[15:22] Samir Shah: Thanks.

[15:24] Call ended.
